review:
[h1]Game Pros[/h1]

• Open world
• Not a GPU/CPU intensive game. Easily runnable and runs quite smooth.
• Beautiful cut scenes/visuals, gorgeous!
• Clean menu.
• Night/Day Cycle.
• Weather does effect how you take on a mission.
• You can easily get immersed in the game and play it for hours without even knowing it.
• Tons of missions and side objectives. Tnere will be plenty to do.
• Everything you do in-game affects the current and future missions.
• Those who can stragically plan better will have an easier time progressing through missions with a higher score.
• Various weapons/tools/items/gear to research. Lots of customization.
• Custmomizable "Mother Base" with soldiers and objects/items from the open world.
• You can infiltrate other players bases and steal soldiers/resources (FoB's/Events alike).
• Multiple companion's that you can bond with throughout missions. (You are not alone!)
• Intelligent and adapatable AI. They will deal with people using repetitive infiltration methods and the like.
• If you punch one of your soldiers in the face, you will recieve words of praise.
• Not a game you can just breeze through in just 10-20 hours.

[h1]Controversial Features[/h1]

• Mission checkpoints can have a large gap, punishing your stupidity and impatience.
• Not necessarily a "Pay to Win" option, but there are microtransactions in this game that 'enhance' your online experience. (MB Coins)

[h1]Game Cons[/h1]

• Storyline seemed to be lacking/repetitive.
• AI and player pathing have a few bugs when encountering ladders or something of the sort in small places (Seldom occurs, but worthwhile to mention).
• Can feel repetitve at times during missions due to similar objectives (Go here and kill/rescure this person, etc).
• Hackers have been spotted while online. (FoB Attacks)
• You CAN NOT bind anything to a numpad key. Which blows for left handed PC gamers.

[h1]Relatable Games[/h1]

• Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes
• Metal Gear (General Franchise)

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

With the ingenuity of Kojima and Co. combined with the power of the Fox engine here is another gem to marvel upon- Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain. The game/franchise as a whole continues to be a lovely experience with a multitude of things to do online post-story. Seriously, you will always have something to do. The story is mesmerizing, leaving you with a feeling of wanting more. For the hardcore Metal Gear fans out there, many of your questions regarding to 'plot holes' will definately get (at least some) answers this time around!

[b]Overall Score: 90/100[/b]

Thank you for reading! Please leave a comment if you feel I have left anything of importance out or if you just want to share your thoughts. Cheers!

[h1]Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain[/h1]

The game is over 6 years old and there is nothing new to say but I still want to add my two cents here. While MGSV has certainly been and still is the benchmark for every stealth game out there in terms of gameplay, it unfortunately falls flat on the core elements that made the franchise so great in the first place. That's the story, the boss fights and the main villain. 
Although I haven't played  its immediate predecessor, Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker, nor the successor MG1, I have multiple playthroughs of MGS1, MGS2, MGS3, and MGS4 over the years. And 100% in MGSV on my PS4 and on Steam.
So, let's break it down a bit.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]

[b]1.) Gameplay:[/b]

Every stealth game fan's wet dream comes true. The possibilities of embarking on a mission are sheer endless. The possible equipment you can use, the items, the weapons, the vehicles, the approach. Everything is there. You can even choose your own "partner". It is the benchmark for the perfect stealth game. Even today.

[b]2.) Immersion and tension when you are on a mission:[/b]

The immersion and tension of a mission are priceless and I haven't played many games where I got the same feel and excitement. When you first play the mission and don't know what to expect, that feeling is just pure gold. The same is true if you play the mission again to find the perfect path and complete your tasks.

[b]3.) Most of the NPCs:[/b]

Well. They do lack some background i have to say. This is even more true if you haven't played any of the other titles in the series or don't want to listen to the hours of recordings that make up most of the background. But they are still well implanted and worth mentioning here.

[b]4.) Base building and the "Forward Operating Base" missions:[/b]

Building a base, watching it grow, with all of the new staff you "recruit" over time is just such a fun part of the game. And so are the FOB missions to get new staff and resources.

[b]5.) Fulton extracts people, animals and vehicles:[/b]

It really never gets boring and I can do that all day.

[b]6.) Quiet and D-Dog[/b]

[h1]Neutral:[/h1]

[b]1.) Side missions:[/b]

Well the side missions are just tedious and there are 157 of them! And without a good way to fast travel, most of them are no fun at all. I would put that in the Cons section, but I needed something for the Neutral section as well. So here we are.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]

[b]1.) Story:[/b]

Some might say the story is fine, I've seen worse and I certainly won't contradict you there, but for MGS standards the story is just underwhelming. Ok. I didn't play Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker, or MG, so I miss some parts of it, but from what I've read, I didn't miss much. Because that's certainly the least interesting part of the MG timeline. There's still potential here, but when you think about the complexity and depth of the previous four MGS games, you can see a huge difference.
There are also plenty of filler missions that completely break the story time after time. If you take away the missions that offer little or no story, there just isn't much left in the end. And when the story finally takes off, which is AFTER the maingame, it just stops with one of the worst cliffhangers in video game history. So sad! 
All that remains is to listen to all the tapes. Which is a must, but you have to spend hours listening to recordings. Hours!

[b]2.) Main villain:[/b]

I don't know how they did this, but they introduced one of the worst villains I have ever met. He's just pathetic, downright boring and can't do anything special. All minor villains outshine the main villain when they first appear on screen. I really have no words for it. 

[b]3.) Boss fights:[/b]

Oh yeah! One of the core elements of the series and some of the most memorable that I have come across in my gaming life. Just think of those epic boss fights against the - more or less - superhuman encounters you've experienced over the years. That epic fight against "The End", or Sniper Wolf, Psycho Mantis, Vamp, Liquid Ocelot, Fatman, Solidus  Snake, or The Boss. These fights very much define the whole series. 
Why they deviated from this path in MGS5 is a mystery to me. Ok, it's more like MGS4 which actually had some good boss fights and maybe they wanted to focus on the missions and stealth gameplay instead. But why not both? Why?
Instead, we don't get any "real" boss fights at all. More like a couple of half boss fights where running away is a better option or even having to run away to advance. And you have to face the same "boss unit" multiple times in the game, even more so with the extrem missions. And when you finally face them for real it is no epic showdown at all. So there is just one real boss fight and that's all. Ok, maybe one and a half. What a weird and weak game design!


[h1]Conclusio:[/h1]

Well, with my 300 hours in the game, I can't really complain. This is mainly due to the incredible fun and addicting gameplay that the game offers. I just wish they had put more effort in the story, boss fights and the main villain, just like in any other Metal Gear Solid game. Recommended at full price and definitely on sale.

[b]Personal Score: 9.5 for the gameplay element. 5.5 for the story, the main villain and the boss fights.[/b]

MGSV builds from a thousand different fundamental components -- simple on their own. Holding enemies up, different "down" conditions, hundreds of tools, commandable allies, etc. Then it plants these ideas in an open environment where enemies will respond consistently to your inputs, throwing a wrench in your best laid plans just often enough to keep things interesting, e.g. night vision if you keep infiltrating at night, helmets if you're going for a lot of tranq darts, etc.

Simply grabbing an enemy from behind can lead to numerous situations and outcomes. You can use them as a human shield, throw them out at their buddies, interrogate them, push them off a cliff... the list really goes on. All these simple parts combining into a whole totally unique to each player. Everyone will inhabit and interact with this world differently -- something really special that most games can't even dream of. It's not as simple as building a character in Skyrim; all that is scripted at the end of the day. i.e. intended by the devs. MGSV has a level of emergence allowing the player to use the tools at their disposal to make their own solutions. It's honestly beautiful.

This game is not for everyone. It's not even for a lot of MG fans. But it's definitely for someone, and if there's a small chance it could be you, don't let this one slip through your fingers.

After gaming for over 20 years, first starting on a SNES controller in the early 90's, I am giving my first gaming review. It is fitting that the first review I write, is the latest of the franchise that I first fell in love with on PS1, the original 'Metal Gear Solid'.

Having played and finished all of the Metal Gear franchise, I can safely assume that I could regard myself as somewhat of a MG seasoned expert and Bottom Line Up Front (BLUF), Hideo Kojima has once again proven that he can easy bring AAA games to the field in a seemingly effortless fashion.

MGSV: The Phantom Pain is a visually pleasing and exciting adventure with a story line that sheds new light on the events of Outer Heaven and Shadow Moses. True to the franchise, stealth is a big part of the game; but not vital. The option to go guns in blazing is there for the times you just get too fed up of failing to infiltrate an enemy base and want to progress.

The combat mechanics of the game are easy to understand and adapt to, even for beginners with varying scales of difficulty. These mechanics are implemented into a very successful multiplayer mode which focuses on both team death match and objective style missions.

Campaign progression introduces multiple new systems of gameplay all the way until the final missions, and although the story is quite linear, there is a extreme level of freedom in regard to choices. Each choice has a consequence, some of which are small and more like an easter egg while others can affect events later in the game. They are not permanent though; all choices can be overturned by replaying particular missions to achieve desired effect.

The map size is incredibly large which can take a substantial amount of time to cross on foot, so there are a variety of vehicles that can be driven across the landscape. The open environment is fantastic for planning and executing missions and the amazing and picturesque graphics feed the desire for those who like to explore. Riding along on horseback, with a rocket launcher in hand shooting at Soviet T-72 tanks whilst listing to a great soundtrack of 80's hits from your Sony walkman is one of the pure gems of this game.

The story, like all Metal Gear games; is the best part of the game. From those that know the background of Naked Snake and his transformation to Big Boss will know the heartfelt detail that was put in to developing individual characters and giving them real human emotion to bring out that of the player. Favourites of the series like Revolver Ocelot and Kaz Miller make a big appearance in the games story along with some new characters like Skull Face and Quiet, which players will come to appreciate.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a master piece and deserves the respect that each of the franchise receives. It is an amazing story that will make you think about warfare and human desire for retribution. This game is one of the best for 2015 and should remain at the top for quite some time.

I give MGSV: The Phantom Pain the following ratings;

10/10       Story
10/10       Gameplay
9.5/10      Graphics
9/10         Soundtrack
9/10         Multiplayer

9.5/10      Overall

Coming from the rest of the series, this game lacks in many areas that make a Metal Gear game. It's the void of quirkiness, for its mood is much too serious. Many times I found myself just riding horseback as Venom Snake listening to Joy Division on the cassettes through Afghanistan and Africa, taking everything in. I felt truly immersed in this world, even when performing the most mundane of actions. The mix of sound design, soundtrack, environments... It's hard to put into words the feeling this game creates.

Oh well, where to start. I'm mindblowingly impressed and also disappointed. I enjoy every minute of it, and I also can't get rid of the awkward feeling when the story unfolds. A story presented in an unmatched quality, but written in the most awkward way. It's going to be a long read, but I'm trying to make it as comprehensive, enjoyable read and well formatted as I can.

[h1]What you get with this game?[/h1]
MGSV above all, is a huge open world freeform game with massive amount of content. You have a huge region in Afganistan and the more lush North-African region to explore, but the gameplay isn't about exploration: as big as these regions are, there aren't many things to see at all. However both regions are filled and get refilled with literally hundreds of sidemissions, kind of Skyrim-way. Not endlessly generated, but mission locations or objectives can repeat even many times, which is the major complaint against this game.

The game's very essence is the freedom you get to achieve your goal whatever way you can. Let your creativity loose. This is something Assassin's Creed has long forgotten, and something MGS's world / age can multiply by x1000. I'm glad the game provides me with a reason to do it, many times.

The point of the massive playfield and the somewhat similar forts, camps etc. is the game has the most mindblowingly incomprehensable freedom. You can play this like you play the better Splinter Cells, or play it as a generic TPS, play it like a master strategist field commander ordering in air strikes, vehicle drop ins from tanks to helicopters to sci-fi walkers raining down death. Not only you can mix these together from second to second, the game has an excellent system for everything to support your style(s) like the game was literally made for that gameplay style, and depending on your actions the game changes in various ways that demands you to adapt one way or another, and it's NEVER game over until you die. 

[h1]Let's go over some examples.[/h1]

[u]You go in stealthy. You are succesful[/u] - you had to watch out for line of sight, noises, enviroment patterns so your camo suit's color aren't green as jungle in the middle of the desert, shadows, covers, enemy communication (not to interrupt people having a radiochat because that raises suspicion), hide bodies, interrogate enemies to get information about nearby specialists, blueprints, mission objectives, guard positions.

[u]You go in stealthy. You fail[/u] - all hells break loose. Enemies reorganize their positions, send out search teams, cover each other, keep communicating and notice if someone isn't checking in, they call in reinforcements from nearby guardposts through radio, if you disabled their communications by destroying the radio station or all the parabole antennes, you can isolate the place from the other bases. Who knows, maybe someone has a flare gun though that others can see and a combat helicopter flies in to swipe the area. 

[u]You go rambo[/u] - You go rambo. With shotguns, granade launchers, rocket launchers, various sci-fi tools like a rocket hand, you can order in a helicopter to cover you while it's loudly playing AMERICAAA F_CK YEAH or any song you choose from the game (oh man those music tapes, masterpiece!) or put in manually. Use a tank if you will, or hijack a local antiair cannon, bash in faces on the run with your metal hand, manipulate weather(! how cool is that?!) and cause a sandstorm that almost blinds and makes enemies deaf for a while while of course having similar effects on you that you can adept to again. Or this may happen randomly. Or you go in stealthy way, but this comes out of it. Anything can happen.

Everything you had to work with before as in noise, cover, hiding bodies, monitoring enemy communication, still applies, always applies, and I just barely mentioned a few systems constantly working in the background. It might be raining, good, your footsteps are hard to hear. It may be night, enemies may or may not have flashlights, you may or may not have an easier time avoiding getting spotted by the deadly helicopter. You may have a tranquilizer pistol, an SMG and some plantable C4 on you, with the combat helicopter above your head. It's not game over, it's not "damn I'm done". 

Figure your way out. Now multiply this by the 2 huge regions, filled with forts, guard stations, mining sites, airplane bases, periodacally changing guard layout and equipment (once they may have helms that prevent you from a silent instant knockout headshot, and suddenly you have to go CQC, massively impacting your plans).

[h1]What else you can do?[/h1]
[u]Main story[/u]
This is where the negatives come to the surface. The directive is to have a small number of long and hands down the best cinematograpy story videos, while 90% of the story of what's going on in the game, what happend before in MGS history, what is happening with MGS history in the background, is all in over a hundred of audiologs. Most of them you get automatically with each storystep, but there are many optional you can find. I'm not a huge fan of this, and while MGS as a franchise is known for it's awkwardly confusing story development, this game isn't only doing it that with the universe of MGS, but also is hardly capable of presenting an enjoyable main story inside this single game unless you do some serious wiki digging and audiolog listening. The story "ends" with Episode 1, that is story mission 31 out of 51. Sadly, KONAMI took away the resources from Kojima and his team to make Episode 2's story just as good (because the story itself is excellent and takes on racism, political power fights, personal revenge, war economy, ethnic cleansing, espionage, sci-fi and somewhat mystical stuff too, it's just difficult to understand.

[u]Base[/u]
If this isn't enough, you have a huge oilrig-like base in the middle of the ocean that can be expanded to many others and being connected to each other. You have a whole RPG / financial management for your base. You can customize everything, and I'm not talking about costumes here and having a red dot sight on or off. Each weapon are made of 10-15 parts that can be changed (and mixed!), your base facilities operate with people you acquire individually based on their skills and your upgrade direction, you can recolor your base, all your weapons, vehicles, you have over 30 different gadgets, tons of vehicles, weapons, each costumizable visually and gameplaywise. The level of customization is unbelivible and so far unmatched in gaming history.

[u]Online[/u] 
You have traditional online versus gameplay modes that are sadly somewhat cheater infected, but there is also another mode that you later unlock with a certain story step in singleplayer. This mode allows you to invade other player's bases, steal their crew, but require extreme caution because getting detected is a huge cutback from score. Many, including me, hate the idea of being able to lose your precious specialists in singleplayer because other players can invade your base while you aren't even playing. Everyone hates it so much that nobody even does it. In my close to 100 playhours I've never once, ever have been invaded. There are always various events that create other PFs (private forces) with their own bases that are NPC owned, and you can invade those for even bigger rewards, and everyone plays these. Everything you can do with your base - set reponse types (lethal / non lethal), your crew's equipment, security devices including sleepgas traps, laser alarms, cameras, drones - they can do it too. 

[h1]The PC version[/h1]
It's swimming in glorious holy lights of the FOX Engine. prime example how to port something to PC. Looks beautiful, easily runs at a set-in-stone 60fps, no hiccups and framedrops at all ever, no weird compatibility issues, no random crashes, no any other issue you can think of. Rare example of absolute perfection.

Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain is a bizarre game to try and talk about because it sits at a particularly awkward crossroads. It is arguably one of the best games of the 2010s, taking the exploding genre of open world games and cracking it open by offering players extreme freedom in the way they tackle tightly-designed missions. This push and pull between developer intention and player choice could have easily been a tension point, but ultimately works because a player’s ability to complete a level is entirely based on their own resourcefulness and creativity. Within a player’s toolkit are nearly infinite ways to complete their mission objective, with the player only being limited by the tools they have on-hand or intrinsic objectives such as high mission rankings or a desired low kill-count. These are all great attributes and are a huge part of why MGSV is hailed today as a masterpiece. 

The issue with that framing is that MGSV doesn’t exist in a vacuum. Kojima’s Metal Gear is perhaps the single most-revered game series in existence, with each one being hailed as a masterpiece of gameplay, storytelling, and technical achievement. As impressive as MGSV is, it is directly competing with its predecessors, and the comparison is not particularly flattering. As fun, slick, and rewarding as its action is, the game’s storytelling and pacing ultimately disrupt that experience in a way the game never really manages to outrun. 

The game is ultimately paced to have two distinct arcs, with one being the effective “main” conflict and the second arc laying the groundwork for how MGSV connects to the rest of the Metal Gear franchise. Of these two arcs, the first is by far the most-interesting, containing 32 episodes with the majority of them containing important story content. While most of these missions are excellent, some really fall short of expectations, leading to a few duds in an otherwise excellent list. And, honestly, if you wanted to check out after Mission 31, I don’t think I would blame you. Most of the story of MGSV is, perhaps intentionally, disjointed, hazy, and dreamlike, intentionally setting up conflicts that connect to the rest of the series. These are largely presented in the form of Mother Base cutscenes, forming a clear and present disconnect between the gameplay and story that the game never manages to shake. 

Perhaps the game’s biggest sin is that it’s simply meandering and filled with padding. Out of the 51 missions (prologue included) present in the main game, 24, by my count, are either challenge missions with specific restrictions in-play, or are completely unrelated to the game’s story and are largely disposable. Most of these missions exist after the conclusion of the first arc; another reason the second arc manages to fall so flat. Of the 19 missions present in the second arc, 15 are of this type, leading to an abysmal 4 main story missions past Mission 31. And, of these 4, one is a partner mission and another is a repeat of a previous mission, just with extra story context added in. This is a huge part of why the back half of the game feels so empty and underwhelming: because nothing you do makes a difference. Much of this is also because the game’s actual conclusion, Mission 51, was never properly finished. There’s a lot of documentation out there online about it, and I would encourage you to check it out if you’re left wanting more after Mission 48. Based on unfinished cutscenes and concept art, it probably would have been the game’s best mission, and I doubt it would have left fans disappointed. 

But even among many of these complaints, I actually have quite a few positive things to say about the game’s story and presentation. I might be alone in thinking this, but I REALLY enjoy MGSV’s codec tapes. The game has a TON of extra context and information contained in tapes players unlock as they progress through missions. Most of these are either designed to further elaborate on cryptic elements of the main game or provide historical context for the larger story, but some of them are also there just as fun side-stories that play out on Mother Base. Of these, my favorite has to be “The Hamburgers of Kazuhira Miller,” which unironically got me to really appreciate fast food burgers. If you can sit through that and not crave a Bic Mac, you are stronger than I am. That said, none of these tapes are necessary for story purposes and you can just as easily ignore them. Perhaps the most-interesting and important tapes are “The Truth” tapes found right at the end of the game. If you’re interested in what happened to the main cast of Snake Eater following MGS Ground Zeroes, they’re worth a listen. 

I also really enjoy how much side content the game has. The game has 157 Side-Ops, most of which are simple side-missions that can be done in the open world. Most of these showcase MGSV at their best, with specific small goals in play that players can attack in any way they want without having to worry about score or rank. There are plenty of duds in this selection, but the vast majority are pretty engaging, with missions like “Eliminate the Armored Vehicle Unit” and “Extract the Highly Skilled Soldier” taking up much of the list. As interesting as side content is in the main world, some of the most-interesting content available takes place on your iDroid. The game has a particularly engaging system of progression, where you work to grow Mother Base and even online content where you can compete to infiltrate each-others bases. I’m not personally that interested in MGSV’s online side, but it can be a huge draw for extending playtime. I know a few people that have put more hours into the game’s online content than the main game, so it’s definitely worth a look.

I want to maintain that MGSV is still one of the best games of its time and absolutely worth a playthrough. But I also want to point out the game’s failures, as I don’t think it is as easy to recommend as many of its series predecessors. If the lack of a solid conclusion to its story and overall emphasis on freedom sound like potential deal-breakers for you, I’m not sure you should bother. Still, even with all its shortcomings, I think MGSV earns its title as a Metal Gear Solid game. It’s not a perfect entry, but it’s a brilliant action game that manages to brilliantly balance an intricately crafted world with deep and rewarding gameplay.

I personally have had very little experience with the Metal Gear franchise previous to 5, most of my exposure was sporadic gameplay of the PS1 game as a child and indirect internet exposure. Recently I acquired a grippling interest in the franchise, chiefly because of the name pattern of the characters that I found very interesting and aesthetic (Solid Snake, Naked Snake, Solidus Snake, Revolver Ocelot, Big boss, etc), previously I thought MGS was just a generic stealth game with a special forces guy infilitrating places and blowing things up on a shallow backdrop setting with obvious bogeys and good guys, I don't need to explain how wrong this notion is. I ended up loving this game so much that I spent hundreds of hours to get the sweet 100% for it (Backup-Backdown Extreme almost induced me into writing a negative review for MGSV, I really want to erase the 10 tries I had to go through that mission to do all it's tasks)

I picked up Ground Zeroes first, it was an absolute blast. The gameplay was breathtaking, the cinematics were on-point. It was a short scenario with around 2 hours worth of gameplay give or take (with several more in the side ops). But I swear to god no game out there has put me "in the scene" as much as Ground Zeroes did. I followed up with getting the Phantom Pain, my start with these games was admittedly somewhat slow, I kind of got bore-bogged in Afghanistan and took a while to slog through that, but once I did, I could not consider myself anymore luckier. MGSV: The Phantom Pain subsequently proved to be one of the funnest games I ever played.


[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]

MGSV has some of the best gameplay I have ever got the pleasure to experience in a video game. The gameplay is extremely nuanced, vibrant and varied. The open world is extremely malleable and can be approached from too many angles/directions for me to describe right now. You start off light, only a few selection of clothes, weapons and equipment. Over the course of the game you'll go from mounting a horse and tranqing people with a low-end WU.Pistol to wearing parasite suits that allow you to become invisible or indestructible, riding a walker gear that can carry flamethrowers, fulton-extract people through metaphysical wormholes, utilise a rocket launcher that can fulton people and throw balloon decoys of yourself that speak short lines like "Kept you waiting, huh" to distract enemy guards. You can slide in cardboard boxes with posters of nude models (or anime girls) on them, you can order your d-dog to stun people with an electric bat, you can call down a thunderstorm that stuns everyone in a 50 meter radius with the highest level stun-arm, you can call weather-modification to induce rain, sandstorms or clear weather, you can also call fire support with chaff that cuts enemy comms, sleeping gas, conventional bombardment, etc. The game is just loaded to the brim with sandbox stuff that you can do and has an amazing and interesting backdrop that is your mother base (struts in the Seychelles that your private army inhabits, you can develop them over the course of the game, fill them with your soldiers that you either kidnap, rescue or recruit, fill them with vehicles and weapons and security cameras to defend them from intruders, and you can visit them and see all this growth in real-time). The controls are amazing (some of the UI and IDroid controls are awkward and stupid, but everything else is fine), the engine is one of the best I have ever got to enjoy, all of this converges into a massive game where you can do a great deal of actions and things and you keep getting even more new toys to play with as you progress the game through development or mother-base growth. The boss fights, as few as they are, are amazing, the Skulls are some of the coolest enemies ever presented in a video game. There are countless mechanics you will discover only after hundreds of hours of playing and cracking all the secret stuff (holding up people with guns, CQC chain take-downs and gun-steals, air-dropping boxes on top of enemies, etc). Your mother base is composed of staff you extract from the battlefield or those that volunteer to your ranks, so a lot of the gameplay involves extracting materials, equipment and soldiers (given they have good stats) to growing your mother base This element might seem tedious to some and fun to others (such as me), so ascertain this is the type of gameplay you are searching for (although you can largely ignore this element of the game, but you will be punished by having the ability to develop less weapons, items and equipment to utilise in the game.


[h1]STORY/LORE[/h1]

This game is widely criticised for having an unfinished story, which I can corroborate. But I still do not feel like it deserves all the flak it gets. The story is there, it's kind-of complete, it has a brutal plot twist in the end, I personally enjoyed it and found it really good (I really love plot twists, so it's subjective). The characters are also one of the biggest carrying weights of Metal Gear Solid V: The -Phantom Pain-. This subtitle almost tells the story on it's own - this game is about the phantom pain, experienced by Venom Snake for losing his arm and his former self, experienced by Kaz for all the limbs he lost (and all the comrades he lost), and finally, experienced by the player, for the big boss he lost. Phantom Pain is this game's story and theme. 
You start-off as Big boss, bed-riddened in a Cypriot hospital, hidden away for the duration of his 9-year long coma after the events of Ground Zeroes, you escape the hospital with the help of a certain Ishmael as Cipher, MSF's old enemy, learns of your where-abouts and attacks the hospital and kills everyone. From there, you go on to rebuild your old Mother base, as things progress, you will find some shocking surprises regarding the origins of your own protagonist, Venom Snake.
I would normally write alot more on the story, but I will not dilate any further on this as I will enter heavy spoiler-territory.

[h1]VISUALS[/h1]

The Fox engine needs no more praise than it receives, it's one of the most breathtakingly cinematic engines, as cinematic as it can get. The lighting alone is stupendous, the textures are (for the most part) amazing, the level of detail on alot of the world is commensurate. But it does feel like there is definitely some level of down-grade from Ground Zeroes (especially in the textures & lighting areas), but overall, it still looks amazing enough that it's easily going to hold up on the visuals department for the next few years. It is easily one of the most beautiful games I have ever enjoyed, and Kojima made no expense or hesitation to make it as beautiful and realistic as possible.

[h1]PERFORMANCE[/h1]

The performance of MGSV is one of it's highest and strongest points, despite being a Japanese console port (which are notoriously under-performing or gimped in some way or another, Nier;Automata and Dark Souls PTDE as examples of this), MGSV has exemplary performance with dips being a rare rarity. I can alt-tab and tumble around in my browser tabs while the game is running at borderless window @ 1440p and be able to tab-back and resume playing seamlessly, in my book, that is a standard for solid video game performance.

There are very rare framerate drops in the games with the usual suspects behind them (Severe dust kick-up, usually from fultoning a cargo container), otherwise, I have absolutely nothing to complain from this game's performance even while playing it supersampled at 4K, a resolution higher than my monitor, and it runs at smooth 60 FPS at all points of the game that matter.

If you are looking for [i]the[/i] perfect open-world game to accompany a months long existential depression, Kojima's ultimate Metal Gear entry will not disappoint. As you wander aimlessly through one of two equally dreary environments, you will have ample time to ponder your place in the universe as Snake similarly struggles to find any cohesive narrative or meaning in this digital masterpiece. Toil furiously to upgrade your weapons, bolster your defenses, and rebuild your mercenary empire. None of your staff will notice or credit you for any of it. There is no reward for your endless labors, and yet you will discover a sort of Nietzschean dignity to the struggle, and through it perhaps see reflected the pointless beauty of your own continued existence.

Metal Gear Solid V is a game that somehow manages to be both a deeply serious war drama and one of the most absurd sandboxes ever designed, where every stupid thing you do becomes a legend. And that contrast is exactly why it works.

I already knew the franchise, and I actually tried MGSV for the first time about eight years ago. And I dropped it, probably too early. Back then, all I really absorbed were the memes and the confusing revelation that more than one Snake exists.

Only after finishing Death Stranding recently did I feel the urge to return to MGSV, and I’m glad I did.

[b]Gameplay[/b]

What makes MGSV exceptional is its sandbox design - a stealth-sandbox hybrid unlike anything I’d played before. Missions can be approached from countless angles. The game just hands you a toolbox and says: "Figure it out". It reminded me of Death Stranding in that sense: the joy of pure autonomy, where every victory feels earned, and every failure becomes your own story.

One of MGSV’s most brilliant achievements is how its anti-war message is expressed not just in dialogue, but directly through gameplay. Enemies adapt to your actions: kill too many, and they start wearing heavy armor and helmets. It’s a subtle, realistic reinforcement of the game’s unspoken rule: "don’t kill unless you must."

Yet the game never forbids combat. In fact, it makes fighting so enjoyable that sometimes it’s hard not to indulge. Especially when it comes to XOF, mercenary executioners with absolutely no humanity. I took enormous satisfaction in hunting them down. I replayed the Skullface mission many times even after I’d stripped the entire base of every resource, probably committing a full-scale mercenary genocide in the process. One-man army delivering justice. And then there’s that infamous ten-minute jeep ride. I didn’t skip it the first three (?) times.

[b]Story and Symbolism[/b]

The story ended up impressing me the most. I absorbed it with genuine delight. I jumped through every bizarre hoop Kojima set up to unlock secret missions and true endings, and I did it willingly.

Even in its hidden content, Kojima’s symbolism shines through. For example, having to defeat Quiet seven times to bring her back. MGSV’s narrative layers reward obsession, and I was happy to indulge.

But what struck me the hardest weren’t the twists or secrets - it was the way the game occasionally drops all irony and reminds you that war isn’t spectacle, but pain you can’t dodge. There are moments when all the absurd freedom of MGSV suddenly collapses into one blunt truth: sometimes you have to do what no one else will. There’s no stealth workaround, no trick, no mercy. Just a decision so heavy it shakes even a legend.

I could talk about the story for hours - but in short, it delivered some of the most memorable emotional beats.

[b]Are there any downsides?[/b]

The game isn’t flawless. Some difficulty spikes - for example, the sudden encounters with the Skulls - felt unfair. The game barely prepares you for them, forcing you to improvise under pressure. Still, these moments rarely overshadow the experience as a whole.

[b]The Vibe[/b]

MGSV has a unique atmosphere - a blend of absurd humor, heavy seriousness, and the exhausted PTSD-soaked aura of a war veteran clinging to whatever humanity he has left.

The game is serious, but it also knows that serious faces are just masks. And sometimes it mocks that seriousness - intentionally and beautifully.

It’s a rare combination: emotional weight and mechanical freedom.
A world where every mistake, every triumph, every random act of stupidity becomes part of Big Boss’s legend - or whoever you choose to be.

[h1]MGSV - A Requiem for a Legend[/h1]
[b]We need to address the heavy heart in the room before we even talk about gameplay. The Phantom Pain isn’t just a game, it is a monument, a farewell, and a beautiful, fractured masterpiece. It is the final Metal Gear Solid project helmed by Hideo Kojima, and let’s be brutally honest, there is no Metal Gear Solid without him. Playing this today, knowing it was the end of that specific, brilliant era, feels like reading a final letter from a mentor. It is a haunting experience, a game that leaves you feeling empty, inspired, and deeply nostalgic all at once.[/b]

[h1]The Sandbox of Our Dreams[/h1]
[b]If you want to talk about raw mechanics, The Phantom Pain is untouchable. It is, quite simply, the greatest stealth-action game ever conceived. The level of player agency here is terrifying, it gives you a massive, open sandbox in Afghanistan or the Angola-Zaire border, drops you in with a pile of gear, and essentially says, "Figure it out."
Whether you want to be a ghost, a tactical mastermind, or a loud, reckless agent of chaos, the game supports you with a level of systems-driven depth that modern games are still struggling to copy. The way the AI adapts to your playstyle is genius. If you start headshotting everyone at night, they’ll start wearing helmets. If you keep using smoke grenades, they’ll equip gas masks. It forces you to evolve, to be creative, and to treat every infiltration like a high-stakes puzzle. It’s an intoxicating loop of planning, execution, and that glorious moment when the plan falls apart and you have to improvise your way out of certain death.[/b]

[h1]A Narrative of Loss and Silence[/h1]
[b]The story of [i]The Phantom Pain[/i] is, much like its protagonist Venom Snake, a ghost. It isn't a loud, exposition-heavy blockbuster like MGS4. Instead, it’s a quiet, introspective journey into trauma, language, and revenge. It’s a tragedy written in silence. Some people complain about the "gaps" in the narrative or the feeling that it was left unfinished, but I think that was always the point.
The game is literally called The Phantom Pain. It’s about the things that are missing, the friends we lost, the limbs we sacrificed, and the legacy that ended too soon. When you listen to the cassette tapes, when you walk through the sterile, industrial halls of Mother Base, you feel the weight of every choice. It is a lonely, melancholic, and deeply profound experience that stays with you long after the final mission ends. It doesn't give you easy answers; it leaves you with scars.[/b]

[h1]Mother Base - The Heart of the Beast[/h1]
[b]Managing Mother Base is a meta-game that could have been a standalone title. Watching your private army grow from a handful of loyalists into a global superpower is an emotional investment. Every soldier you fulton out of the field isn't just a number, they are a recruit you saved, someone who now owes you their life. When things go wrong, or when you’re forced to face the harsh realities of your mission, it hurts. You aren't just playing a soldier, you are the Commander, the Big Boss, the man who lost everything. The bond you feel with your staff, with D-Dog, and even with the crumbling foundations of your own organization is a testament to Kojima’s ability to make us care about the mundane.[/b]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
[b][i]METAL GEAR SOLID V: THE PHANTOM PAIN[/i] is a flawed, brilliant, and deeply emotional farewell. It’s a testament to a visionary who dared to make games that weren't just "content," but pieces of art that challenged our morality and our understanding of heroism. We will never see another Metal Gear like this because we will never see another project lead by Hideo Kojima in this universe again. It’s a phantom limb, you feel the ache of its absence, but you cherish the memory of what it was.
